source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 20 (PDF 156-168, printed 152-164); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 20 (Medical Physics), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.
Medical Physics: Introduction and Radiations Used

blocks.prompt: 1 Medical physics is the branch of physics that applies physical principles and techniques to:

options.text: medicine, especially the diagnosis and treatment of diseases
the design of bridges and buildings
the study of stars and galaxies

blocks.explanation: Medical physics applies physical principles and techniques to medicine, especially in the diagnosis and treatment of diseases (introduction).

book_ref.quote: Medical physics is a branch of physics that applies physical principles and techniques to medicine

blocks.prompt: 2 Medical physics plays an important role in modern healthcare mainly by:

options.text: increasing the radiation dose given to every patient
making surgery necessary for every diagnosis
improving imaging accuracy, reducing radiation risks and enhancing treatment methods

blocks.explanation: It improves the accuracy of medical imaging, reduces radiation risks and enhances treatment methods (introduction).

book_ref.quote: by improving the accuracy of medical imaging, reducing radiation risks, and enhancing treatment methods

blocks.prompt: 3 According to the chapter's introduction, positron emission tomography (PET) works through:
blocks.explanation: PET works through positron–electron annihilation and detection of the gamma rays produced (introduction).

book_ref.quote: works through positron–electron annihilation and gamma-ray detection

blocks.prompt: 4 Techniques such as X-ray imaging, ultrasound, CT and PET allow doctors to study internal organs:
blocks.explanation: These techniques let doctors detect fractures, diagnose tumors and study internal organs without surgery (introduction).

book_ref.quote: These techniques allow doctors to detect fractures, diagnose tumors, and to study internal organs without surgery.

blocks.prompt: 5 Radiation is the transfer of energy through space or matter in the form of:
blocks.explanation: Radiation is the transfer of energy through space or matter in the form of waves or particles (introduction).

book_ref.quote: Radiation is the transfer of energy through space or matter in the form of waves or particles.

blocks.prompt: 6 Ionizing radiation is radiation that has enough energy to:

options.text: change the shape of a crystal
remove electrons from atoms, producing ions

blocks.explanation: Ionizing radiation has enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, producing ions; non-ionizing radiation does not (introduction).

book_ref.quote: Ionizing radiation has enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, producing ions.

blocks.prompt: 7 Which of the following is a non-ionizing radiation used in medical physics?
blocks.explanation: Ultrasound waves and radiowaves are non-ionizing; X-rays, gamma rays and positrons are the ionizing examples (introduction).

book_ref.quote: examples of non-ionizing radiations are ultrasound waves and radiowaves

blocks.prompt: 8 X-rays and gamma rays interact with matter through:

options.text: the photoelectric effect and Compton scattering

blocks.explanation: Interaction of X-rays and gamma rays with matter occurs through the photoelectric effect and Compton scattering (introduction).

book_ref.quote: Interaction of X-rays and gamma rays with matter occurs through photoelectric effect and Compton scattering.

blocks.prompt: 9 In medical physics, the positrons used for imaging are emitted from:

options.text: the heated filament of an X-ray tube

blocks.explanation: The positrons are emitted from radioactive tracers (introduction; used in PET, 20.5).

book_ref.quote: The positrons are emitted from radioactive tracers.

blocks.prompt: 10 When non-ionizing waves such as ultrasound and radiowaves interact with matter, they are:
blocks.explanation: Non-ionizing waves are reflected, refracted or absorbed when they interact with matter (introduction).

book_ref.quote: These waves are reflected, refracted, or absorbed when these interact with the matter.

blocks.prompt: 11 Gamma rays are used in nuclear medicine, such as PET scans and cancer treatment, because of their:
blocks.explanation: Gamma rays are used in nuclear medicine and cancer treatment due to their high penetrating power (introduction).

book_ref.quote: due to their high penetrating power

blocks.prompt: 12 Radiowaves are used in medical imaging in the technique of:
blocks.explanation: Radiowaves are used in MRI, where they interact with atomic nuclei to image soft tissues without harmful radiation (introduction).

book_ref.quote: Radiowaves are used in techniques such as MRI

blocks.prompt: 13 In MRI, radiowaves help produce detailed images by interacting with:
blocks.explanation: In MRI, radiowaves produce detailed images by interacting with atomic nuclei (introduction).

book_ref.quote: by interacting with atomic nuclei

blocks.prompt: 14 The dual role of an ultrasound transducer is that it:

options.text: generates X-rays and detects gamma rays
heats the tissue and measures its temperature
injects a tracer and detects positrons
generates ultrasound waves and detects the reflected signals

blocks.explanation: The transducer generates ultrasound waves and also detects the reflected signals from inside the body (20.1).

book_ref.quote: The transducer plays a dual role; it generates ultrasound waves and detects the reflected signals from inside the body.

blocks.prompt: 15 Ultrasound imaging is described in the chapter as a technique that is:
blocks.explanation: Ultrasound is a widely used, non-invasive imaging technique for tissues, organs and the fetus (20.1).

book_ref.quote: Ultrasound is a widely used, non-invasive medical imaging technique

blocks.prompt: 16 The Greek word "piezein", from which "piezoelectric" is formed, means:
blocks.explanation: "Piezein" means "to press"; "electric" refers to the production of electricity (20.1).

book_ref.quote: comes from the Greek word "piezein," which means "to press"

blocks.prompt: 17 The piezoelectric effect was discovered in 1880 by:
blocks.explanation: It was discovered in 1880 by two French scientists, Pierre Curie and Jacques Curie (20.1).

book_ref.quote: This effect was discovered in 1880 by two French scientists, Pierre Curie and Jacques Curie.

blocks.prompt: 18 Which set of crystals did the Curie brothers experiment with?
blocks.explanation: They experimented with quartz, tourmaline and Rochelle salt (20.1).

book_ref.quote: They were experimenting with crystals such as quartz, tourmaline, and Rochelle salt

blocks.prompt: 19 Rochelle salt, one of the piezoelectric crystals, is chemically:
blocks.explanation: Rochelle salt is sodium potassium tartrate (20.1).

book_ref.quote: Rochelle salt (sodium potassium tartrate)

blocks.prompt: 20 The piezoelectric material PZT, shown in the chapter's figure of the effect, is:
blocks.explanation: PZT is lead zirconate titanate (Fig. 20.1, as corrected in the book-correction box) (20.1).

book_ref.quote: the material is lead zirconate titanate (PZT)

blocks.prompt: 21 The piezoelectric effect occurs in crystals that:

options.text: have a perfect centre of symmetry

blocks.explanation: Piezoelectric crystals have no centre of symmetry and contain small regions of positive and negative charge (20.1).

book_ref.quote: These crystals have no centre of symmetry

blocks.prompt: 22 In a piezoelectric crystal, an electric field appears on the surface when pressure is applied because:

options.text: the balance of positive and negative charges is disturbed and the charges move slightly

blocks.explanation: Normally the charges are balanced; pressure disturbs the balance, the charges move slightly and a field appears on the surface (20.1).

book_ref.quote: Normally, these charges are balanced, but when pressure is applied, the balance is disturbed

blocks.prompt: 23 Production of an electric field on the surface of a crystal when mechanical pressure is applied is called the:
blocks.explanation: Pressure producing an electric field is the direct piezoelectric effect (20.1).

book_ref.quote: This is called the direct piezoelectric effect.

blocks.prompt: 24 When an electric field is applied to a piezoelectric crystal, it changes shape a little. This is the:
blocks.explanation: A change of shape caused by an applied electric field is the converse piezoelectric effect (20.1).

book_ref.quote: This is called the converse piezoelectric effect.

blocks.prompt: 25 The piezoelectric effect makes it possible to turn:

options.text: pressure into voltage and voltage into pressure

blocks.explanation: It turns pressure into voltage and vice versa; this is how ultrasound "talks" to the body (20.1).

book_ref.quote: The piezoelectric effect makes it possible to turn pressure into voltage and vice versa.

blocks.text: 20.2 Diagnostic Use of Ultrasound in Medical Imaging

blocks.prompt: 26 The ultrasound waves sent into the body for imaging typically have frequencies in the range:
blocks.explanation: Ultrasound imaging uses high frequency sound waves, typically 1 MHz-15 MHz (20.2).

book_ref.quote: typically in the range of 1 MHz-15 MHz

blocks.prompt: 27 A key advantage of ultrasound imaging is that it is safe and repeatable because:

options.text: it uses very high energy X-rays
it does not use ionizing radiation

blocks.explanation: Ultrasound does not use ionizing radiation, which makes it safe, non-invasive and repeatable (20.2).

book_ref.quote: it does not use ionizing radiation and making it a safe, non-invasive, and repeatable imaging method

blocks.prompt: 28 Part of an ultrasound wave is reflected when it meets a boundary between two tissues that have different:
blocks.explanation: At a boundary between tissues of different acoustic impedances, part of the wave is reflected (20.2).

book_ref.quote: When these waves encounter a boundary between two tissues with different acoustic impedances

blocks.prompt: 29 The acoustic impedance of a tissue is determined by:

options.text: tissue density and the speed of sound in it
the atomic number of the contrast medium

blocks.explanation: Acoustic impedance is determined by tissue density and sound speed (20.2).

book_ref.quote: (determined by tissue density and sound speed)

blocks.prompt: 30 In receive mode, the ultrasound transducer detects the reflected waves using the:
blocks.explanation: The transducer switches to receive mode and detects the reflected waves using the direct piezoelectric effect (20.2).

book_ref.quote: detects these reflected waves using the direct piezoelectric effect

blocks.prompt: 31 To construct an ultrasound image, the computer uses the returning echoes':
blocks.explanation: A computer calculates the time delay and intensity of the returning echoes to construct the image (20.2).

book_ref.quote: a computer calculates the time delay and intensity of the returning echoes

blocks.prompt: 32 In an ultrasound image, areas that produce stronger reflections appear:
blocks.explanation: Areas with stronger reflections appear brighter, revealing internal structures (20.2).

book_ref.quote: Areas with stronger reflections appear brighter in the image

blocks.prompt: 33 The ultrasound pulses emitted by the transducer travel through the body:

options.text: at the speed of light in all tissues
at exactly the same speed in all tissues
at different speeds depending on the type of tissue

blocks.explanation: The pulses travel at different speeds depending on the type of tissue they pass through (20.2).

book_ref.quote: which travel at different speeds depending on the type of tissue they pass through

blocks.prompt: 34 According to the chapter, the crystals in an ultrasound probe are:

options.text: able only to send sound, not detect it
smaller than a grain of rice, yet both send and detect sound

blocks.explanation: The probe's crystals are smaller than a grain of rice but can both send and detect sound waves (20.2).

book_ref.quote: The crystals in an ultrasound probe are smaller than a grain of rice

blocks.prompt: 35 An ultrasound probe works at 5.0 MHz in soft tissue where the speed of sound is 1540 m s⁻¹. Using v = fλ, the wavelength of the waves in the tissue is:

book_ref.quote: It operates by sending high frequency sound waves

blocks.prompt: 36 An echo from an organ boundary returns to the transducer 104 μs after the pulse is sent. If sound travels at 1540 m s⁻¹ in the tissue, the depth of the boundary is about:
blocks.explanation: The pulse goes and returns, so depth = vt/2 = 1540 × 104 × 10⁻⁶ / 2 = 0.080 m = 8.0 cm (20.2).

book_ref.quote: The reflected echoes are then collected and analyzed to create an image.

blocks.prompt: 37 In obstetrics, ultrasound is used to:

options.text: monitor fetal growth and estimate gestational age

blocks.explanation: In obstetrics it monitors fetal growth, estimates gestational age and identifies abnormalities during pregnancy (20.2).

book_ref.quote: it helps monitor fetal growth, estimate gestational age

blocks.prompt: 38 Echocardiography, an ultrasound technique, is used in cardiology to evaluate:

options.text: the tracer uptake in the brain
the X-ray attenuation of the lungs
the heart's structure and function in real time

blocks.explanation: Echocardiography lets doctors evaluate the heart's structure and function in real time (20.2).

book_ref.quote: In cardiology, echo cardiography allows doctors to evaluate

blocks.prompt: 39 Which group of organs is examined by ultrasound in the abdominal region?

options.text: Liver, kidneys, gallbladder, pancreas and bladder

blocks.explanation: In the abdominal region ultrasound examines the liver, kidneys, gallbladder, pancreas and bladder (20.2).

book_ref.quote: such as the liver, kidneys, gallbladder, pancreas, and bladder

blocks.prompt: 40 In the musculoskeletal system, ultrasound aids in detecting:
blocks.explanation: In the musculoskeletal system it detects ligament injuries, joint inflammation and other soft tissue conditions (20.2).

book_ref.quote: it aids in detecting ligament injuries, joint inflammation

blocks.prompt: 41 In urology, ultrasound is used to examine:

options.text: the prostate, testicles and urinary system

blocks.explanation: Urology uses ultrasound to examine the prostate, testicles and urinary system (20.2).

book_ref.quote: The field of urology also benefits from ultrasound

blocks.prompt: 42 Stronger echoes and clearer boundaries in an ultrasound image are produced when the two tissues have:

options.text: a larger difference in acoustic impedance

blocks.explanation: A higher acoustic impedance difference (e.g. soft tissue and bone) gives stronger echoes and clearer boundaries (20.2).

book_ref.quote: A higher difference between two tissues (e.g., soft tissue and bone) causes stronger echoes

blocks.prompt: 43 Compared with low frequency ultrasound, high frequency ultrasound gives:
blocks.explanation: Higher frequency gives better resolution but less penetration; lower frequency penetrates deeper with lower clarity (20.2).

book_ref.quote: Higher frequency ultrasound offers better resolution but less penetration

blocks.prompt: 44 To image an organ lying deep inside the body, the better choice is ultrasound of:

options.text: lower frequency, accepting lower image clarity
any frequency, since depth does not matter

blocks.explanation: Lower frequency waves penetrate deeper, though with lower image clarity (20.2).

book_ref.quote: lower frequency waves penetrate deeper but have lower image clarity

blocks.prompt: 45 A special gel is applied between the ultrasound transducer and the skin in order to:

options.text: remove air gaps and improve transmission of the sound waves

blocks.explanation: The gel removes air gaps and improves the transmission of sound waves (20.2).

book_ref.quote: to remove air gaps and improve sound waves transmission

blocks.prompt: 46 Ultrasound can measure the speed of blood flow by detecting shifts in sound frequency. This uses the:
blocks.explanation: Ultrasound measures blood flow speed using the Doppler effect, by detecting shifts in sound frequency (20.2).

book_ref.quote: measure blood flow speed using the Doppler effect

blocks.prompt: 47 Taking the speed of sound in tissue as 1540 m s⁻¹ and v = fλ, the wavelength of 12 MHz ultrasound is:
blocks.explanation: λ = v/f = 1540 / (12 × 10⁶) = 1.28 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.128 mm. The shorter wavelength of high frequency goes with better resolution (20.2).

book_ref.quote: Frequency of Ultrasound: Higher frequency ultrasound

blocks.prompt: 48 Transitions of electrons in hydrogen or other light elements give spectral lines in the:
blocks.explanation: Small energy differences in light elements give lines in the infrared, visible or ultraviolet region (20.3).

book_ref.quote: result in the emission of spectral lines in the infrared, visible or ultraviolet region

blocks.prompt: 49 In a heavy atom, the electron shell closest to the nucleus is the:
blocks.explanation: The shells are labelled K, L, M, N, O, ...; the K-shell is closest to the nucleus (20.3).

book_ref.quote: The K-shell being closest to the nucleus

blocks.prompt: 50 Transitions of inner-shell electrons in heavy atoms give X-rays rather than visible light because the inner electrons are:

options.text: loosely bound, so the energy differences are small
tightly bound, so the energy differences involved are large
free electrons like those in metals

blocks.explanation: Inner-shell electrons are tightly bound and need a large energy to displace; on return, photons of large energy (X-rays) are emitted (20.3).

book_ref.quote: The inner shell electrons are tightly bound

blocks.prompt: 51 The X-rays from inner-shell transitions are called characteristic X-rays because they:

options.text: consist of a series of specific wavelengths or frequencies
come only from the hydrogen atom

blocks.explanation: They consist of series of specific wavelengths or frequencies, hence the name characteristic X-rays (20.3).

book_ref.quote: These X-rays consist of series of specific wavelengths or frequencies

blocks.prompt: 52 The study of characteristic X-ray spectra has played an important role in the study of:

options.text: atomic structure and the periodic table

blocks.explanation: Characteristic X-ray spectra helped in the study of atomic structure and the periodic table (20.3).

book_ref.quote: has played a very important role in the study of atomic structure and the periodic table

blocks.prompt: 53 A transition in a light atom releases a photon of energy 1.9 eV. Taking h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, its wavelength is about:

book_ref.quote: due to small energy differences in the transition levels

blocks.prompt: 54 An inner-shell transition in a heavy atom emits a photon of energy 8.0 keV. With h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, its wavelength is:

book_ref.quote: photons of larger energy are emitted

blocks.prompt: 55 X-rays are produced in an X-ray tube, which is a:
blocks.explanation: The arrangement consists of a high vacuum tube called the X-ray tube (20.3).

book_ref.quote: It consists of a high vacuum tube called X-ray tube.

blocks.prompt: 56 In an X-ray tube, electrons are emitted by the:
blocks.explanation: The cathode, heated by the filament F, emits electrons which are accelerated towards the anode T (20.3).

book_ref.quote: When the cathode is heated by the filament F.

blocks.prompt: 57 If V is the potential difference between cathode and target, the maximum kinetic energy with which an electron (charge e) strikes the target is:

book_ref.quote: the (K.E.)ₘₐₓ with which the electron strikes the target is given by

blocks.prompt: 58 The target in an X-ray tube is made of:
blocks.explanation: The fast electrons strike a target made of tungsten or any other heavy element (20.3).

book_ref.quote: strike a target made of tungsten or any other heavy element

blocks.prompt: 59 Electrons in an X-ray tube are accelerated through 30 kV. Taking e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the maximum kinetic energy with which they strike the target is:

book_ref.quote: Suppose that these fast moving electrons of energy Ve strike a target

blocks.prompt: 60 A Kα X-ray photon is emitted when an electron jumps:

options.text: from the K-shell to the L-shell
from the L-shell into a hole in the K-shell
from the M-shell into the K-shell

blocks.explanation: An L-shell electron filling a K-shell hole emits the Kα X-ray, hf = E_L − E_K (Eq. 20.2) (20.3).

book_ref.quote: The electron from the L-shell jumps to occupy the hole in the K-shell

blocks.prompt: 61 The energy of a Kβ X-ray photon is given by:
blocks.explanation: When an M-shell electron fills the K-shell hole, hf(Kβ) = E_M − E_K (Eq. 20.3) (20.3).

book_ref.quote: It is also possible that the electron from the M-shell might also jump

blocks.prompt: 62 For the same target, how does the Kβ photon compare with the Kα photon?

options.text: Kβ has higher energy and shorter wavelength
Kβ has lower energy and longer wavelength
Both have exactly the same energy

blocks.explanation: The M-shell lies above the L-shell, so E_M − E_K > E_L − E_K: Kβ has more energy and a shorter wavelength than Kα (20.3).

book_ref.quote: the photons emitted in this M → K transition are Kβ X-rays

blocks.prompt: 63 X-rays from inner-shell transitions are called characteristic X-rays because their energies depend upon:

options.text: the size of the X-ray tube

blocks.explanation: Their energies depend upon the type of target material, so they are characteristic of it (20.3).

book_ref.quote: because their energies depend upon the type of target material

blocks.prompt: 64 On a graph of X-ray intensity against wavelength, characteristic X-rays appear as:

options.text: a continuous band with no lines
discrete lines on a continuous spectrum
lines only in the visible region

blocks.explanation: Characteristic X-rays appear as discrete lines on a continuous spectrum (Fig. 20.6) (20.3).

book_ref.quote: The characteristic X-rays appear as discrete lines on a continuous spectrum

blocks.prompt: 65 After a K-shell hole is filled from the L or M shell, the new holes in the L and M shells are:

options.text: filled by electrons from higher states, creating more X-rays
filled by protons from the nucleus

blocks.explanation: The holes in the L and M shells are occupied by transitions from higher states, creating more X-rays (20.3).

book_ref.quote: The holes created in the L and M shells are occupied by transitions

blocks.prompt: 66 In a target atom E_K = −58.0 keV and E_L = −8.0 keV. The energy of the Kα photon is:

book_ref.quote: thereby emitting a photon of energy hf, called the Kα X-ray given by

blocks.prompt: 67 In a target atom E_K = −58.0 keV and E_M = −2.0 keV. With h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, the wavelength of the Kβ X-ray is:

book_ref.quote: The photons emitted in such transitions i.e., inner shell transitions are called characteristic X-rays

blocks.prompt: 68 The continuous X-ray spectrum is due to an effect known as:
blocks.explanation: The continuous spectrum is due to bremsstrahlung or braking radiation (20.3).

book_ref.quote: The continuous spectrum is due to an effect known as bremsstrahlung or braking radiation.

blocks.prompt: 69 Electrons striking the target emit bremsstrahlung because:

options.text: an accelerating (here strongly decelerating) charge emits electromagnetic radiation

blocks.explanation: An accelerating charge emits electromagnetic radiation; the electrons are strongly decelerated by the target (20.3).

book_ref.quote: We know that an accelerating charge emits electromagnetic radiation.

blocks.prompt: 70 Bremsstrahlung from an X-ray target lies in the X-ray region because:

options.text: the rate of deceleration is so large that the radiation has short wavelength

blocks.explanation: Since the rate of deceleration is so large, the emitted radiation has short wavelength, in the X-ray region (20.3).

book_ref.quote: Since the rate of deceleration is so large

blocks.prompt: 71 The shortest wavelength λmin of the continuous X-ray spectrum is produced when an electron:

options.text: loses only a little energy in each of many collisions
loses all its kinetic energy in the first collision

blocks.explanation: If an electron loses all its K.E. in the first collision, (K.E.)max = hf_max; this f_max corresponds to λmin (20.3).

book_ref.quote: In the case when the electrons lose all their kinetic energy in the first collision

blocks.prompt: 72 Electrons that suffer a number of collisions before coming to rest give X-rays of:
blocks.explanation: Such electrons give photons of smaller energy, i.e. X-rays of longer wavelength, filling the continuous spectrum (20.3).

book_ref.quote: This will give rise to photons of smaller energy or X-rays of longer wavelength.

blocks.prompt: 73 Electrons are accelerated through 25 kV in an X-ray tube. With h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the minimum wavelength of the X-rays is:

book_ref.quote: the entire kinetic energy appears as a X-ray photon

blocks.prompt: 74 An X-ray tube works at 50 kV. With h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the maximum frequency in its continuous spectrum is:

book_ref.quote: When the fast moving electrons bombard the target, they are suddenly slowed down

blocks.prompt: 75 If the accelerating potential difference of an X-ray tube is doubled, the minimum wavelength λmin of the continuous spectrum:
blocks.explanation: Ve = hf_max = hc/λmin, so λmin = hc/(Ve) ∝ 1/V; doubling V halves λmin (20.3).

book_ref.quote: Thus the continuous spectrum is obtained due to deceleration of impacting electrons.

blocks.prompt: 76 The loss of energy by X-rays as they travel through the body and interact with atoms is called:
blocks.explanation: As X-rays travel through the body they lose energy by interacting with atoms; this is attenuation (20.3).

book_ref.quote: This process is called attenuation.

blocks.prompt: 77 X-rays transfer energy to the atoms of the body mainly by:

options.text: ionizing them, i.e. knocking out electrons

blocks.explanation: X-rays can ionize atoms by knocking out electrons, which is how energy is transferred (20.3).

book_ref.quote: X-rays can ionize atoms; it means that they knock out electrons

blocks.prompt: 78 As an X-ray beam passes through a material, its intensity decreases:

options.text: as the square of the thickness

blocks.explanation: The intensity decreases gradually, following an exponential pattern (20.3).

book_ref.quote: This drop follows an exponential pattern.

blocks.prompt: 79 The correct attenuation law for an X-ray beam of initial intensity I₀ passing through thickness x of a material is:
blocks.explanation: I = I₀e^(−μx); the thickness x appears only in the exponent (the printed extra x is a misprint) (20.3).

book_ref.quote: The correct law is I = I₀e^(−μx)

blocks.prompt: 80 In the attenuation law, the attenuation coefficient μ depends on:

options.text: the material and the X-ray energy
only the thickness of the material

blocks.explanation: μ is the attenuation coefficient, which depends on the material and the X-ray energy (20.3).

book_ref.quote: attenuation coefficient (depends on the material and X-ray energy)

blocks.prompt: 81 An X-ray beam passes through 1.0 cm of a tissue whose attenuation coefficient is 50 m⁻¹. Using I = I₀e^(−μx), the fraction I/I₀ that emerges is about:

book_ref.quote: x = thickness of the material (in metres)

blocks.prompt: 82 For which thickness of a material with μ = 25 m⁻¹ does the X-ray intensity fall to I₀/e (about 37% of I₀)?

book_ref.quote: I = intensity after passing through material

blocks.prompt: 83 Image intensifiers are used in fluoroscopy (real-time X-ray imaging) to:

options.text: brighten the image and so reduce radiation exposure

blocks.explanation: Image intensifiers brighten the image, making it easier to see and helping reduce radiation exposure (20.3).

book_ref.quote: Image intensifiers are used in real-time X-ray imaging (fluoroscopy).

blocks.prompt: 84 In X-ray images, the term contrast means:

options.text: how clearly different tissues can be told apart
the frequency of the X-ray tube supply

blocks.explanation: Contrast means how clearly we can tell different tissues apart; it depends on the X-ray energy (20.3).

book_ref.quote: Contrast in X-ray images means how clearly

blocks.prompt: 85 Hard X-rays (high energy) are used mainly for imaging:
blocks.explanation: Hard (high energy) X-rays are used for bone imaging; soft X-rays suit soft tissues (20.3).

book_ref.quote: Hard X-rays (high energy) are used for bone imaging.

blocks.prompt: 86 For X-ray imaging of soft tissue such as the breast, the better choice is:
blocks.explanation: Soft X-rays (low energy) are better for soft tissues like the breast (20.3).

book_ref.quote: Soft X-rays (low energy) are better for soft tissues like the breast.

blocks.prompt: 87 Which substances are used as X-ray contrast media?
blocks.explanation: Contrast media are substances like iodine (Z = 53) or barium (Z = 56) that absorb X-rays well (20.3).

book_ref.quote: special substances like iodine (Z = 53) or barium (Z = 56)

blocks.prompt: 88 Contrast media make tissues stand out more clearly in X-ray images because they:

options.text: have low atomic numbers and let X-rays pass
have high atomic numbers and increase X-ray absorption

blocks.explanation: Having high atomic numbers, they increase X-ray absorption and make tissues stand out (20.3).

book_ref.quote: Since they have high atomic numbers, they increase X-ray absorption

blocks.prompt: 89 Computed tomography (CT) is an imaging technique that combines:
blocks.explanation: CT combines X-ray technology with computer processing to give cross-sectional and 3D images (20.4).

book_ref.quote: combines X-ray technology with computer processing

blocks.prompt: 90 In an ordinary chest X-ray, it is difficult to tell the front and back ribs apart because:

options.text: the image is flat (2D) and the structures overlap

blocks.explanation: An ordinary X-ray gives a flat 2D image in which bones and organs overlap (Fig. 20.7) (20.4).

book_ref.quote: it's difficult to tell the front and back ribs apart

blocks.prompt: 91 After a CT scanner has made the image of one slice, it:

options.text: moves slightly along the body and repeats for the next slice

blocks.explanation: The scanner moves slightly along the body and repeats the process; all the slices are combined into a 3D image (20.4).

book_ref.quote: the scanner moves slightly along the body and repeats the process for the next slice

blocks.prompt: 92 In the CT machine described in the chapter:

options.text: the patient rotates while the X-ray tube is fixed
the X-ray tube rotates around the patient while the detectors stay in place
neither the tube nor the detectors move
a gamma source rotates inside the patient

blocks.explanation: The X-ray tube rotates around the patient while detectors stay in place, collecting information from all sides (Fig. 20.8) (20.4).

book_ref.quote: the X-ray tube rotates around the patient while detectors stay in place

blocks.prompt: 93 The radiation used by a CT scanner comes from:

options.text: a radioactive tracer inside the patient

blocks.explanation: A CT scanner uses X-rays from an X-ray tube with detectors opposite the tube (the printed 'gamma ray' label is a misprint) (20.4).

book_ref.quote: A CT scanner uses X-rays from an X-ray tube

blocks.prompt: 94 The Greek word "tomos", from which tomography is named, means:
blocks.explanation: Tomography comes from the Greek word tomos, meaning slice: the body is imaged layer by layer (20.4).

book_ref.quote: Tomography: From the Greek word tomos, meaning slice.

blocks.prompt: 95 In "Computed Axial Tomography", the word axial means that:

options.text: the patient spins on an axle
the scan is taken along the body's axis
only the axial skeleton is imaged
X-rays travel along the tube's axis only

blocks.explanation: Axial: the scan is taken along the body's axis (a line through the body) (20.4).

book_ref.quote: Axial: The scan is taken along the body's axis

blocks.prompt: 96 The CT scanner was invented in the early 1970s by:
blocks.explanation: Sir Godfrey Hounsfield (England) and Allan Cormack (South Africa) invented the CT scanner in the early 1970s (20.4).

book_ref.quote: The CT-scanner was invented by Sir Godfrey Hounsfield

blocks.prompt: 97 Hounsfield and Cormack were awarded the Nobel Prize for the CT scanner in:
blocks.explanation: Both were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1979 (20.4).

book_ref.quote: awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1979

blocks.prompt: 98 According to the chapter, CT scans are crucial in treating strokes because they can:

options.text: detect a stroke within minutes of onset
detect it only after several weeks

blocks.explanation: CT scans can detect strokes within minutes of onset, which is crucial for lifesaving treatment (20.4).

book_ref.quote: CT-scans can detect strokes within minutes of onset

blocks.prompt: 99 A single ordinary X-ray image is quick to produce, but its limitation is that it gives:

options.text: a moving real-time picture of blood flow

blocks.explanation: Single X-ray images give only a flat, two-dimensional view; CT gives three-dimensional images (20.4).

book_ref.quote: they only give a flat, two-dimensional view

blocks.prompt: 100 With CT, doctors can distinguish between tissues even when the tissues have:
blocks.explanation: CT makes it easier to distinguish tissues even when they have very similar densities (20.4).

book_ref.quote: This makes it easier to distinguish between tissues, even when they have very similar densities.

blocks.prompt: 101 A CT image showing the exact position and size of a tumor helps doctors to:

options.text: accurately target the tumor with high-energy X-rays or gamma rays

blocks.explanation: Knowing the tumor's position and size helps doctors accurately target it with high-energy X-rays or gamma rays (20.4).

book_ref.quote: a CT scan can clearly show the position and size of a tumor

blocks.prompt: 102 The main risk of a CT scan to the patient is that it:
blocks.explanation: CT involves exposure to X-rays, a form of ionizing radiation, which carries a small risk (20.4).

book_ref.quote: CT scans involve exposure to X-rays, which are a form of ionizing radiation

blocks.prompt: 103 Doctors take special precautions with CT scans especially for:

options.text: pregnant women and patients with existing health concerns

blocks.explanation: Because of the ionizing radiation, special precautions are taken especially for pregnant women or patients with health concerns (20.4).

book_ref.quote: especially when scanning pregnant women

blocks.prompt: 104 A CT scanner builds a 3D model of the body by:

options.text: combining many 2D cross-sectional slices, like stacking layers of a cake
taking one X-ray from the front
detecting photon pairs from a tracer

blocks.explanation: It reconstructs 2D cross-sections from many angles; combining the slices gives a 3D model, like stacking layers of a cake (20.4).

book_ref.quote: like stacking layers of a cake

blocks.prompt: 105 In nuclear medicine, the radiation that forms the image originates:

options.text: from an X-ray tube outside the patient
inside the patient, from an administered radiopharmaceutical

blocks.explanation: In nuclear medicine the radiation originates inside the patient from an administered radiopharmaceutical (20.5).

book_ref.quote: the radiation originates inside the patient from an administered radiopharmaceutical

blocks.prompt: 106 In nuclear medicine, the detected signal mainly reflects:

options.text: physiological function rather than only anatomy

blocks.explanation: The signal reflects physiological function rather than only anatomy (20.5).

book_ref.quote: the detected signal reflects physiological function rather than only anatomy

blocks.prompt: 107 In SPECT (Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography):

options.text: a gamma-emitting tracer is used and a rotating gamma camera records many projection views
a positron tracer is used with a ring of coincidence detectors
an X-ray tube rotates around the patient

blocks.explanation: In SPECT a gamma-emitting tracer is introduced and a rotating gamma camera records projection views, reconstructed into cross sections (20.5).

book_ref.quote: a gamma-emitting tracer is introduced into the body and a rotating gamma camera records many projection views

blocks.prompt: 108 PET differs from SPECT mainly in that PET uses:
blocks.explanation: PET extends the SPECT idea using positron-emitting tracers (20.5).

book_ref.quote: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) extends this idea using positron-emitting tracers

blocks.prompt: 109 After positron-electron annihilation in PET, the two gamma photons travel:

options.text: at right angles to each other
in random directions with no relation

blocks.explanation: Annihilation produces two gamma photons emitted in nearly opposite directions (20.5).

book_ref.quote: producing two gamma photons emitted in nearly opposite directions

blocks.prompt: 110 PET is valuable because it images:

options.text: only air spaces in the lungs
metabolic and biochemical activity at the cellular/molecular level

blocks.explanation: PET images metabolic and biochemical activity at the cellular/molecular level (20.5).

book_ref.quote: images metabolic and biochemical activity at the cellular/molecular level

blocks.prompt: 111 Which use of PET is mentioned in the chapter?
blocks.explanation: PET is valuable for early cancer detection and staging, brain function and cardiac abnormalities (20.5).

book_ref.quote: highly valuable for early cancer detection and staging

blocks.prompt: 112 In a PET scan, the radioactive tracer is:

options.text: applied as a gel on the skin
injected into a vein in a small amount

blocks.explanation: A small amount of radioactive tracer is injected into a vein and carried by the blood (20.5).

book_ref.quote: a small amount of radioactive tracer is injected into a vein

blocks.prompt: 113 The PET tracer builds up more in:

options.text: very active tissues, such as many cancers or working parts of the brain and heart

blocks.explanation: The tracer builds up more in very active tissues such as many cancers or working parts of the brain and heart (20.5).

book_ref.quote: builds up more in tissues that are very active

blocks.prompt: 114 A positron emitted by the tracer:

options.text: travels out of the body before annihilating
is detected directly by the ring
travels only a short distance before meeting an electron

blocks.explanation: Each positron travels only a short distance before meeting an electron in nearby tissue (20.5).

book_ref.quote: Each positron travels only a short distance before meeting an electron

blocks.prompt: 115 In a PET scanner, the detectors are arranged:

options.text: in a ring around the patient

blocks.explanation: Detectors in a ring around the patient detect the photon pairs and send signals to a computer (20.5).

book_ref.quote: Detectors arranged in a ring around the patient

blocks.prompt: 116 Brighter areas on a PET image show regions of:

options.text: higher tracer concentration and higher tissue activity

blocks.explanation: Brighter areas correspond to higher tracer concentration and therefore higher tissue activity (20.5).

book_ref.quote: Brighter areas on the PET image correspond to regions of higher tracer concentration

blocks.prompt: 117 A positron and an electron (each of mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg) annihilate at rest. Taking c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and that each photon carries the energy of one particle's mass, the energy of each gamma photon is:
blocks.explanation: E = mc² = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × (3.00 × 10⁸)² = 8.20 × 10⁻¹⁴ J for each photon (about 0.51 MeV) (20.5).

book_ref.quote: their mass is converted into energy in the form of two gamma-ray photons

blocks.prompt: 118 Radiotherapy for cancer makes use of:

options.text: high energy particles to kill tumor cells with minimal harm to healthy tissue

blocks.explanation: Radiotherapy uses high energy particles to kill tumor cells with minimal harm to healthy tissues (20.5).

book_ref.quote: makes use of high energy particles to kill tumor cells

blocks.prompt: 119 Radiation therapy in which the radiation is delivered from a machine positioned outside the body is called:
blocks.explanation: In teletherapy the radiation is delivered externally from a machine outside the body (20.5).

book_ref.quote: radiation is delivered externally from a machine positioned outside the body

blocks.prompt: 120 In brachytherapy, the radioactive source is:

options.text: kept in a machine far outside the body
applied as gel on the skin
inserted inside or close to the tumor

blocks.explanation: In brachytherapy a radioactive source is inserted inside or close to the tumor (20.5).

book_ref.quote: a radioactive source is inserted inside or close to the tumor

blocks.prompt: 121 In the oncology team, medical physicists specialize in:

options.text: equipment quality assurance, treatment time, treatment planning and dose mapping

blocks.explanation: They handle equipment quality assurance, calculation of treatment time, treatment planning and mapping of dose distribution (20.5).

book_ref.quote: they specialize in equipment quality assurance

blocks.prompt: 122 To make every radiation treatment safe and effective, medical physicists work hand in hand with:

options.text: radiation oncologists, dosimetrists and laboratory technicians

blocks.explanation: They work with radiation oncologists, dosimetrists and laboratory technicians (20.5).

book_ref.quote: They work hand in hand with radiation oncologists, dosimetrists, and laboratory technicians
